newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thyssen-Krupp steel titan rattles Germany.
newsitem.headline: Thyssen-Krupp steel titan rattles Germany.

text.p: Thousands of angry German steelworkers stayed off the job Thursday to protest a pact between steelmakers Thyssen and Krupp that will create a new steel giant but cost 8,000 jobs.
Workers at three Krupp Hoesch steel mills were on strike in an attempt to secure written confirmation of management pledges that none of them would lose their jobs.

The new joint venture merger, which began as a bank-financed $8 billion hostile takeover bid by Krupp, will create a behemoth that can spew out 15 million tons of steel a year, equal to France's Usinor-Sacilor or British Steel .

Two other areas where Thyssen and Krupp Hoesch already cooperate will not be part of the deal: Krupp Thyssen Nirosta, the world's biggest stainless steel maker, which is controlled by Krupp, and a Thyssen-led tinplate venture.

The new company, Thyssen Krupp Stahl AG, will concentrate hot metal operations at Thyssen's main Duisburg steel works, shutting down three blast furnaces at Krupp's Dortmund plant, and expand rolling and processing activities at Krupp Hoesch.

Thyssen will hold 60 percent of the new company and Krupp Hoesch will hold a 40 percent share. The deal could achieve annual savings of 550 million marks ($325 million), analysts say, to help finance the job cuts and trim the combined work force to 18,000.
The companies have promised there will be no compulsory layoffs, but economists, like the striking workers, questioned whether Thyssen and Krupp would be able to keep their word.

"This promise is an uncovered check for the future," said Heinz Schrumpf of the Rheinisch Westfaelisches economic institute, which specialises in the steel industry. "I have my doubts that compulsory layoffs can be ruled out as easily as the workers think."

The new job cuts are just the latest in a wave of consolidation that began with West Germany's first postwar steel crisis in 1975. The industry then began a bloodletting that slashed the work force of nearly 350,000 to 110,000 by 1995 at the end of the most recent steel slump.

Restructuring in the former East Germany has been just as severe. There were 80,000 steel workers in the east at the end of 1989, just before German unification in 1990, compared with around 10,000 today.
Cuts in jobs and production in the steel sector, unforeseen just two weeks ago, will have a broad impact on coal mining as the steel industry's demand for coke falls with output cuts.

Unemployment in the Ruhr, Germany's "rust belt," already stands at 15.3 percent, three points above the national average, at a time when the number of unemployed has reached a level not seen since 1933.
Any increase in aid to Germany's smokestack industries is unwelcome as Bonn seeks to cut spending and avert the threat of failing to qualify for Europe's single currency.
